title: The Hebrew alphabet
summary: The 22 letters and their sounds, the five final forms, look-alike letters, and how to read Hebrew without vowel points.

sections.h: Twenty-two letters, read from right to left
sections.body:
Hebrew is written and read from right to left, so a Hebrew book opens at what an English reader would call the back. There are no capital letters, and in print the letters stand separately. (Handwriting uses a cursive script whose letters look quite different; the shapes here are the print forms you see on signs, on screens and in books.)

All 22 letters are consonants, but four of them — א, ה, ו, י — also help to show vowels (see 'Reading without vowel points' below). Learn the letter names as well as the sounds: on the phone, Israelis spell a name out letter by letter — כהן: kaf, hey, nun sofít.

Digits and words in Latin letters keep their own left-to-right order inside a Hebrew line: הפגישה בשעה 10:00 (hapgishá besha'á éser) — The meeting is at 10:00.
table: silent or a glottal stop; carries a vowel
h; usually silent at the end of a word
v; also shows the vowels o and u
y; also shows the vowel i
silent or a glottal stop for most speakers (some say it deep in the throat); carries a vowel
r, made at the back of the throat (like French r)

sections.h: Five letters change shape at the end of a word
sections.body:
Five letters have a special final form (sofít, 'final'), used only as the last letter of a word. The sound stays the same; only the shape changes. Four of them — ך, ן, ף, ץ — have a long leg that reaches below the line, while ם is closed like a box.

When an ending is added, the letter is no longer last, so it goes back to its normal shape: שולחן → שולחנות (shulkhanót) tables, עץ → עצים (etsím) trees.

ך and ף always sound kh and f. A few loanwords end in a p sound; they are written with the ordinary פ, because ף can only be f: ג׳יפ (jip) jeep.

sections.h: One letter, two sounds — one sound, several letters
sections.body:
Three letters have two pronunciations: ב is b or v, כ is k or kh, and פ is p or f. In texts with vowel points, a dot inside the letter (dagesh) shows b, k, p; ordinary text has no dots, so you learn each word's sound together with the word. Some guidelines:
• At the start of a word they are normally b, k, p: בית (báyit) house, כלב (kélev) dog, פה (po) here.
• At the end of a word they are normally v, kh, f: טוב (tov) good; ך and ף are always kh and f.
• Inside a word either is possible: שבת (shabát) Shabbat, but חבר (khavér) friend; מפה (mapá) map, but שפה (safá) language. It can change even within one family of words: ספר (séfer) book, but מספר (mispár) number.
• Loanwords go their own way: פלאפל (faláfel) starts with f, פיצה (pítsa) with p.

ש also has two sounds: sh (shin), as in שלום, and s (sin), as in ישראל (yisra'él) and עשר (éser) ten. sh is much more common.

The other side of the coin: in modern Israeli speech several sounds can be written with more than one letter, because sounds that were once different have merged. You can't hear the spelling, so learn the spelling of each word with the word itself.

Several letters differ only in a small detail. At first, look closely at the groups in the table; after a few weeks of reading, your eye does it automatically.

A useful trick is to learn one short word for each pair, such as בן / כן or דרך, and picture it whenever you're unsure.
table: ב sits on a flat base that sticks out at the bottom right; כ is rounded at the bottom
ד has a sharp corner sticking out at the top right; ר is rounded; ך is the final form and its leg goes below the line
ה has a gap at the top left; ח is closed at the top; ת has a small foot at the bottom left
הם (hem) they · חם (kham) hot · תה (te) tea
ו is a straight stroke down to the line with a small head; ז has a cap that sticks out on both sides; ן is the final form and goes below the line
ס is rounded at the bottom; ם is square and appears only at the end of a word
ע has two arms joined at the bottom, with a tail slanting down to the left; צ sits flat on the line, with a small arm at the top right
י is short and hangs from the top of the line; ו reaches all the way down

sections.body:
Vowel points (niqqud), the dots and dashes above and below the letters, appear in children's books, poetry, prayer books and dictionaries. Everyday Hebrew — signs, newspapers, websites, text messages — is written without them. Instead, some letters help to show the vowels:
• ו shows o or u: טוב (tov) good, שוק (shuk) market, הוא (hu) he.
• י shows i, and also ei: שיר (shir) song, תיק (tik) bag, איפה (éifo) where.
• At the end of a word, ה (and sometimes א) shows a or e: תודה (todá) thank you, יפה (yafé) beautiful, אבא (ába) dad.
• A word that begins with a vowel sound starts with א or ע: אני (aní) I, אוכל (ókhel) food, עברית (ivrít) Hebrew.
• Inside a word, a ו or י that is a real consonant (v, y) is usually doubled: שווה (shavé) worth, עייף (ayéf) tired. At the start or the end of a word one letter is enough: ילד (yéled) child, קו (kav) line.

The vowels a and e are usually not written inside a word, so a short word can sometimes be read in more than one way: ספר is séfer (book) or sapár (barber). The sentence tells you which, and this is normal for Israelis too. With practice you'll recognise common words as whole shapes, the way you read English.

This full spelling with extra ו and י (ktiv male) is the standard for everyday writing: שולחן, היום, מיד, כמובן.

Hebrew has no letters for the sounds j (as in 'jeans'), ch (as in 'chips') and zh (as in 'measure'). Loanwords and foreign names show them with a geresh ׳ after ג, צ or ז:
• ג׳ = j: ג׳ינס (jins) jeans, ג׳ירפה (jiráfa) giraffe
• צ׳ = ch: צ׳יפס (chips) chips, fries; צ׳ק (chek) cheque
• ז׳ = zh: ז׳קט (zhakét) jacket, בז׳ (bezh) beige

A geresh also shortens a single word: גב׳ כהן (gvéret kóhen) Ms Cohen; רח׳ הרצל (rekhóv hértsl) Herzl St. And the letters double as numbers — א׳ = 1, ב׳ = 2, ג׳ = 3 — so the days of the week are often written יום א׳ (Sunday, read yom rishón or yom álef), יום ב׳ (Monday).

Gershayim ״ — two strokes placed before the last letter — mark an abbreviation made of several words. Some are read as the full words, others as a word of their own:
• ת״א = תל אביב (tel avív)
• בי״ס = בית ספר (bet séfer) school
• מע״מ (ma'ám) VAT
• מנכ״ל (mankál) CEO
• ש״ח = שקל חדש, the shekel; in prices people simply say shékel: 20 ש״ח (esrím shékel)

On a phone or computer keyboard people often type ' and " instead; you'll see both in everyday writing.

drills.en: Shalom (hello; peace).
drills.explain: At the end of a word מ is written ם (mem sofít): שלום.

drills.en: Table.
drills.explain: At the end of a word נ is written ן, with a leg below the line: שולחן. In the plural שולחנות it is no longer last, so it goes back to נ.

drills.en: Money.
drills.explain: An f at the end of a word is written ף (pey sofít): כסף.

drills.en: Country; land.
drills.explain: At the end of a word צ is written ץ (tsádi sofít): ארץ.

drills.en: Way; road.
drills.explain: A kh written with כ becomes ך at the end of a word: דרך. Note the look-alikes in this one word: ד, ר and ך.

drills.en: Yes.
drills.explain: כן (ken) begins with כ. With ב it would be בן (ben), son: ב has a base that sticks out at the bottom right, while כ is rounded.

drills.en: Hot.
drills.explain: חם (kham) begins with ח, which is closed at the top. ה, with a gap at the top left, would give הם (hem), they.

drills.en: Tea.
drills.explain: תה (te): ת has a small foot at the bottom left, ה has a gap at the top. The final ה is silent; it only shows the vowel e.

drills.en: Song.
drills.explain: Without niqqud the vowel i is shown with י: שיר.

drills.en: Market.
drills.explain: ו shows the vowels o and u: שוק.

drills.en: Thank you.
drills.explain: תודה is spelled with ת. ת and ט both sound t, so each word's spelling has to be learned; ת is much more common.

drills.en: Write in Hebrew: ani (I).
drills.hint: starts with א, ends with the vowel letter י
drills.explain: אני: א carries the opening a, נ is n, and י shows the final i. A word that starts with a vowel sound begins with א or ע.

drills.en: Write in Hebrew: shalom (hello).
drills.hint: four letters, ending in a final form
drills.explain: שלום: ש (sh) + ל (l) + ו (the vowel o) + ם (final mem). The a isn't written.

drills.en: Write in Hebrew: kafe (coffee).
drills.hint: k is ק; the final e is ה
drills.explain: קפה: ק (k) + פ (p, here f) + ה, which shows the final e. The a isn't written.

drills.en: Write in Hebrew: chips (fries).
drills.hint: ch is צ׳; i is י
drills.explain: The sound ch is written צ with a geresh: צ׳יפס. The i is shown by י, and the word ends in ס.

drills.prompt: כתבו בעברית את הקיצור של תל אביב: ___
drills.en: Write the Hebrew abbreviation for Tel Aviv.
drills.explain: ת״א = תל אביב: the first letters of the two words, with gershayim ״ before the last letter.

title: I, you, he: pronouns and sentences without 'to be'
summary: The ten personal pronouns, sentences with no verb 'to be' (אני מורה, היא מחיפה), זה / זאת / אלה, saying no with לא, and the first question words.

sections.body:
English has seven personal pronouns; Hebrew has ten, because it marks gender not only in 'he' and 'she' but also in 'you' and in the plural 'you' and 'they'. Only אני (I) and אנחנו (we) are the same for men and women.

• 'You' to one person: אתה (atá) to a man, את (at) to a woman. The ה of אתה is silent; it only shows the final a. To a woman you ask את ישראלית? (at yisre'élit?), to a man אתה ישראלי? (atá yisre'éli?) — Are you Israeli?
• Plural 'you' and 'they': אתם (atém) and הם (hem) are for men or for mixed groups — a single man in the group makes it masculine. אתן (atén) and הן (hen) are for women only. In casual speech you'll often hear אתם and הם for women too, but write אתן and הן.
• הוא and היא also mean 'it', because every noun is masculine or feminine (see the next lesson): איפה הספר? — הוא על השולחן. (éifo haséfer? — hu al hashulkhán) — Where's the book? — It's on the table.
• Don't confuse את (at, 'you') with the little word את (et) that marks a direct object: same letters, a different word. You'll meet it later in the course.

Hebrew has no present tense of 'to be'. You simply put the subject next to what you say about it — a noun, an adjective or a place — and there is no word for 'a' / 'an' either:
• אני סטודנט. (aní studént) — I'm a student. (a man speaking)
• אני סטודנטית. (aní studentít) — I'm a student. (a woman speaking)
• היא מחיפה. (hi mekháifa) — She's from Haifa.
• סמיר רופא. (samír rofé) — Samir is a doctor.
• הקפה טוב. (hakafé tov) — The coffee is good.
• אנחנו בעבודה. (anákhnu ba'avodá) — We're at work.

The noun or adjective matches the subject in gender and number: a woman says אני סטודנטית, a man says אני סטודנט, and a group of friends says אנחנו סטודנטים (anákhnu studentím).

When the second half is itself definite — a name, or a noun with ה — Hebrew normally adds הוא, היא, הם or הן as a link; without it you'd have a phrase rather than a sentence: דני הוא המנהל. (dáni hu hamenahél) — Dani is the manager. Compare דני, המנהל… — Dani, the manager…

The link is also common, though optional, after a name or a longer subject: ישראל היא ארץ קטנה. (yisra'él hi érets ktaná) — Israel is a small country.

'To be' does appear in the past and the future (הייתי, I was; אהיה, I'll be). That comes in A2.

sections.h: זה, זאת, אלה: this is, these are
sections.body:
To point at something or someone, use זה, זאת or אלה — again with no verb:
• זה (ze) for a masculine noun: זה הבית שלי. (ze habáyit shelí) — This is my house.
• זאת (zot) for a feminine noun: זאת דנה, החברה שלי. (zot dána, hakhaverá shelí) — This is Dana, my friend.
• אלה (éle) for any plural: אלה ההורים שלי. (éle hahorím shelí) — These are my parents.

In this use Hebrew doesn't distinguish 'this' from 'that': זה covers both. You'll also see and hear זו (zo) for זאת and אלו (élu) for אלה; they mean the same and sound a little more formal.

In questions and general remarks people use זה for almost everything: מה זה? (ma ze?) — What's this? זה בסדר. (ze beséder) — It's fine. When you ask about a person, match the gender: מי זה? (about a man), מי זאת? (about a woman).

Don't confuse זה ספר (This is a book — a whole sentence) with הספר הזה (haséfer hazé — this book), where זה follows the noun and takes ה, like an adjective. More on that in the next lesson.
table: זה המחשב שלי. — This is my computer.
זאת המורה שלי. — This is my teacher. (a woman)
אלה החברים שלי. — These are my friends.

sections.body:
לא (lo) means both 'no' and 'not'. In a sentence without a verb, put לא right before the part you're denying — normally straight after the subject:
• אני לא מורה. (aní lo moré) — I'm not a teacher.
• זה לא קפה, זה תה. (ze lo kafé, ze te) — This isn't coffee, it's tea.
• הם לא בבית. (hem lo babáyit) — They're not at home.

As an answer, לא comes first, followed by a comma: את מחיפה? — לא, אני מעכו. (at mekháifa? — lo, aní me'áko) — Are you from Haifa? — No, I'm from Acre. And of course: לא, תודה. (lo, todá) — No, thank you.

Formal written Hebrew has a special negative for these sentences, אינו / אינה (he isn't / she isn't), which you'll meet later in the course. For speech and everyday writing, לא is all you need.

A yes/no question uses exactly the same words as the statement; only your voice rises at the end (and in writing you add a question mark):
• אתה מתל אביב. (atá mitel avív) — You're from Tel Aviv.
• אתה מתל אביב? — Are you from Tel Aviv?

(In formal writing such a question often opens with האם (ha'ím): האם אתה מתל אביב?)

Question words come at the start of the sentence, and there is still no verb 'to be': מי זה? — Who's that? איפה הבנק? — Where's the bank?

מאיפה is מ (from) + איפה (where). מ is a prefix, written together with the next word: מחיפה, מתל אביב, מרוסיה, מאתיופיה. Its vowel changes in speech (mi-, me-), but in writing it's always just מ. So the answer to מאיפה also uses מ: מאיפה אתה? — אני מאשדוד. (me'éifo atá? — aní me'ashdód) — Where are you from? — I'm from Ashdod.

Other question words work the same way: מתי (matáy) when, למה (láma) why, איך (eikh) how, כמה (káma) how much / how many.
table: מי המנהל? (mi hamenahél?) — Who's the manager?
מה השם שלך? (ma hashém shelkhá? / shelákh?) — What's your name? (to a man / to a woman)
איפה השירותים? (éifo hasherutím?) — Where are the toilets?
מאיפה את? (me'éifo at?) — Where are you from? (to a woman)

drills.en: Dani, are you from Tel Aviv?
drills.explain: To one man, 'you' is אתה (atá). There's no 'are': אתה מתל אביב?

drills.en: Miriam, are you a teacher?
drills.explain: To one woman, 'you' is את (at) — with no ה at the end.

drills.en: This is Abebe. He's an engineer.
drills.explain: הוא (hu) = he. No 'is' and no 'an': הוא מהנדס = he's an engineer.

drills.en: This is Rana. She's a doctor.
drills.explain: היא (hi) = she. The noun is feminine as well: רופאה (rof'á).

drills.en: We're students at the university.
drills.hint: 'we' — the same for men and women
drills.explain: אנחנו (anákhnu) is 'we' for men and women alike; the noun after it is plural: סטודנטים. (אנו is a formal written variant.)

drills.en: Maya and Shira, are you friends?
drills.explain: To a group of women only, 'you' is אתן (atén). In casual speech you'll hear אתם too, but אתן is the correct form.

drills.en: Igor and Michal? They're at work.
drills.hint: a man and a woman together
drills.explain: A mixed group takes the masculine plural: הם (hem).

drills.en: Katya and Ruti? They're at home.
drills.explain: For women only, 'they' is הן (hen).

drills.en: This is my house.
drills.explain: בית is masculine, so 'this is' is זה (ze). זהו (zéhu, from זה + הוא) is a slightly more emphatic variant.

drills.en: This is my mum, Shoshana.
drills.explain: For a woman or a feminine noun, 'this is' is זאת (zot); זו (zo) is also correct, a little more formal.

drills.en: These are my friends from work.
drills.explain: For any plural, 'these are' is אלה (éle); אלו (élu) is also used.

drills.en: I'm not from Haifa, I'm from Acre.
drills.explain: Put לא (lo) before the part you deny: אני לא מחיפה.

drills.prompt: ___ זה? — זה לא קפה, זה תה. (what)
drills.en: What's this? — It's not coffee, it's tea.
drills.explain: מה (ma) asks 'what?'. The answer uses לא: זה לא קפה.

drills.en: Who's that? — That's my uncle.
drills.explain: מי (mi) asks about people; מה asks about things.

drills.en: Where's the central bus station?
drills.explain: איפה (éifo) asks 'where?' — and there's no 'is'. (היכן means the same in formal Hebrew.)

drills.en: Where are you from? — I'm from Beersheba.
drills.explain: מאיפה (me'éifo) = from where: the prefix מ + איפה. The answer uses מ as well: מבאר שבע. (Formal Hebrew also has מהיכן.)

title: Masculine, feminine and plural
summary: Every noun is masculine or feminine; plurals in ־ים and ־ות and the common irregular ones; adjectives that agree; and the definite article ה.

sections.h: Every noun is masculine or feminine
sections.body:
In Hebrew every noun — not only people, but also things, places and ideas — is either masculine or feminine. The ending usually tells you which:
• Feminine: nouns ending in a stressed ־ה (-a) or in ־ת: משפחה (mishpakhá) family, עבודה (avodá) work, מכונית (mekhonít) car, מחברת (makhbéret) notebook, דלת (délet) door.
• Masculine: everything else: ספר (séfer) book, מחשב (makhshév) computer, שולחן (shulkhán) table, רחוב (rekhóv) street.

Exceptions, to learn one by one:
• Feminine with no feminine ending: עיר (ir) city, ארץ (érets) country, דרך (dérekh) way, road — and most body parts that come in pairs: יד (yad) hand, רגל (régel) leg, foot, עין (áyin) eye, אוזן (ózen) ear.
• Masculine although they end in ת or ה: בית (báyit) house, שירות (sherút) service, צוות (tsevét) team, where the ת belongs to the root; לילה (láyla) night, where the a is unstressed; and nouns ending in an e sound, such as שדה (sadé) field.

For people, the gender follows the person, and most words for people have a feminine form with ־ה, ־ת or ־ית. A few look the same in writing: מורה is moré (a male teacher) or morá (a female teacher).

The basic rule: masculine nouns add ־ים (-im); feminine nouns replace their ־ה or ־ת with ־ות (-ot), and ־ית becomes ־יות (-iyot).

Three things to notice:
• The stress moves to the ending, and the vowels inside the word often change: yéled → yeladím, séfer → sfarím. Without niqqud you only see the ending change.
• A final letter becomes a regular letter when an ending is added: עץ → עצים.
• A mixed group takes the masculine plural: ילדים is boys or children in general, and תלמידים pupils of both sexes; ילדות and תלמידות are girls only.

sections.h: Irregular plurals: learn them with the noun
sections.body:
Some nouns take the 'wrong' plural ending. Their gender doesn't change — only the ending looks surprising — so adjectives still follow the real gender (see the next section): שולחנות גדולים (big tables), ערים גדולות (big cities).

• Masculine nouns with ־ות: שולחן → שולחנות, מקום → מקומות (place), חלון → חלונות (window), כיסא → כיסאות (chair), לילה → לילות (night), אבא → אבות (father; in casual speech you'll also hear אבאים, 'dads').
• Feminine nouns with ־ים: עיר → ערים, שנה → שנים (year), מילה → מילים (word), ביצה → ביצים (egg).
• Plurals that change more than the ending: אישה → נשים (woman), איש → אנשים (man; the plural means 'people'), בית → בתים (house), יום → ימים (day), אמא → אמהות (mother).

Good dictionaries give the plural with every noun: learn the two together.

sections.h: Adjectives agree in gender and number
sections.body:
An adjective comes after its noun and copies the noun's gender and number, with the same four endings you know from nouns: no ending (m. sg.), ־ה (f. sg.), ־ים (m. pl.), ־ות (f. pl.).

• The adjective follows the noun's real gender, not its ending: שולחנות גדולים (shulkhanót gdolím) big tables; ערים יפות (arím yafót) beautiful cities; נשים חכמות (nashím khakhamót) clever women.
• The vowels inside the adjective shift too: גדול (gadól) → גדולה (gdolá); קטן (katán) → קטנה (ktaná).
• Adjectives ending in ־ה look the same in the masculine and feminine singular: בית יפה (báyit yafé), עיר יפה (ir yafá); in the plural, יפים and יפות.

The same agreement applies when the adjective is the predicate (remember: no 'is'): הילד קטן (hayéled katán) — The boy is small; הדירה גדולה (hadirá gdolá) — The apartment is big; הספרים חדשים (hasfarím khadashím) — The books are new.
table: ילד קטן (yéled katán) a small boy
ילדה קטנה (yaldá ktaná) a small girl
ילדים קטנים (yeladím ktaním) small boys, small children

sections.body:
Hebrew has no word for 'a': ספר is 'a book'. 'The' is ה (ha-), written together with the noun, and it's the same for every gender and number: הספר (haséfer) the book, הדירה (hadirá) the apartment, העיר (ha'ír) the city, הנשים (hanashím) the women.

• An adjective that describes a definite noun takes ה as well: דירה חדשה (a new apartment) → הדירה החדשה (hadirá hakhadashá) the new apartment.
• So one letter separates a phrase from a sentence: הילד הקטן = the small boy, but הילד קטן = The boy is small.
• Names of people and of most places are definite already and don't take ה: דנה, חיפה, ישראל.
• 'This' in the sense of 'this book' also comes after the noun, with ה: הספר הזה (haséfer hazé), הדירה הזאת (hadirá hazót), הילדים האלה (hayeladím ha'éle).
• After ב (in, at), ל (to) and כ (like), the ה drops out of writing but its a stays in the prefix: ב + הבית → בבית (babáyit) at home, in the house; ב + העבודה → בעבודה (ba'avodá) at work.

drills.en: I have a new computer.
drills.explain: מחשב is masculine singular, so the adjective has no ending: חדש (khadásh).

drills.en: A small boy and a small girl.
drills.explain: ילדה is feminine singular, so the adjective adds ־ה: קטנה (ktaná).

drills.en: Small boys and small girls.
drills.explain: ילדות is feminine plural, so the adjective takes ־ות: קטנות (ktanót).

drills.en: This shop has books in Hebrew and in English.
drills.explain: ספר is masculine, so its plural adds ־ים: ספרים (sfarím).

drills.en: Lots of young families live in our neighbourhood.
drills.explain: A feminine ־ה becomes ־ות: משפחות (mishpakhót). The verb גרות and the adjective צעירות are feminine plural too.

drills.en: There are lots of cars on my street.
drills.explain: Nouns ending in ־ית make their plural in ־יות: מכוניות (mekhoniyót).

drills.en: There are tables and chairs in the classroom.
drills.explain: שולחן is masculine but takes ־ות: שולחנות (shulkhanót), just like כיסא → כיסאות. The final ן becomes נ, because it's no longer at the end.

drills.en: Haifa and Beersheba are big cities.
drills.explain: עיר is feminine, but its plural ends in ־ים: ערים (arím), and the י drops out. The adjective stays feminine: גדולות.

drills.en: There are men and women on the course.
drills.explain: אישה has a completely different plural: נשים (nashím).

drills.en: Dani and Yossi are good fathers.
drills.explain: אבא is masculine and its plural is אבות (avót); the adjective stays masculine: אבות טובים. In casual speech you'll also hear אבאים.

drills.en: They have a big house with a garden.
drills.explain: בית ends in ת, but that ת is part of the root: the noun is masculine, so גדול (gadól).

drills.en: Israel is a small country.
drills.explain: ארץ has no feminine ending, but it is feminine, so the adjective is קטנה (ktaná).

drills.en: Jerusalem and Acre are beautiful, ancient cities.
drills.explain: ערים ends in ־ים, but עיר is feminine, so the adjective is feminine plural: יפות (yafót), like עתיקות.

drills.en: The tables in the classroom are old.
drills.explain: שולחן is masculine, so even with ־ות the adjective takes ־ים: ישנים (yeshaním).

drills.en: The apartment is small but comfortable.
drills.explain: 'The' is the prefix ה: הדירה (hadirá). קטנה has no ה, so this is a full sentence: the apartment is small.

drills.en: The new books are on the table.
drills.explain: A definite noun needs a definite adjective: הספרים החדשים (hasfarím hakhadashím). Without the second ה, הספרים חדשים would mean 'The books are new'.
